en: The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgataguhyagarbha Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Records of the Three Qin.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].
There were eight thousand bhikṣus in the assembly;

and thirty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—renowned by all, who had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), subdued Māra and his enemies, and had attained complete mastery over all dharmas;
they were highly skilled in various supernatural transformations and manifestations.

They possess skillful knowledge of all dhyānas and samādhis, entering and emerging from them with mastery; they act as uninvited friends to all sentient beings, forever free from the hindrances and entanglements;
they are adept at discerning the faculties of all beings;

they skillfully rely upon the definitive teachings (nītārtha), purify the six perfections (pāramitās) to reach the further shore, and sport in the five supernormal powers (abhijñās); they teach and transform sentient beings without weariness of mind, having long cultivated various practices for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, and having already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.

They are well-protected and sustained by all Buddhas; they guard the city of the True Dharma and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed; they constantly gladden all beings with their noble virtues and turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma.

They are skillfully able to travel to and fro through boundless Buddha-fields to pay homage to the Buddhas, letting out the great lion’s roar, repairing the great ship of the Dharma, beating the great drum of the Dharma, and blowing the great conch of the Dharma.
They skillfully accumulate all adornments of merit and virtue, adorning their bodies with the primary and secondary marks, and possess firm progress in mindfulness and wisdom.

They possess a thorough knowledge of shame and remorse, delighting themselves in the joy of the Dharma; they are fully endowed with and have accomplished great loving-kindness and great compassion. They eclipse all the radiance of the sun and moon and cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas—gain and loss, disrepute and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure;

they are neither elated nor depressed. Having skillfully severed craving and anger, they are constantly in accord with skillful means and wisdom. According to the faculties of sentient beings, they skillfully transform and guide them, rescuing those who are without rescue. Whatever they do, they observe with careful discernment; thus their actions of body, speech, and mind are free from all faults and afflictions.

They are well able to gather the adornments of meditative concentration and wisdom; their minds are harmonious and supple like great dragons, and like great lions, they subdue the followers of external paths.
They are well able to advance toward the conduct of great beings and remain free from all fears;
they are well able to decisively sever the doubts of all sentient beings;
and they are well able to exhort immeasurable Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma.
They are well-established in great vows and forever free from the two views; they constantly and diligently strive to deliver all sentient beings;
they skillfully know the causes and conditions arising from defilement and purity;

they skillfully cultivate right mindfulness, giving rise to no thoughts of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and never abandoning the jewel-mind of omniscience. Their minds are pure like space; their bodies are supple; their minds are undefiled and their resolve is indestructible. Wherever they go, their minds are free from attachment. Their wondrous voices are harmonious and gentle; whatever they speak is clear and easy to understand. Their words are pure and white, expounding untainted dharmic verses. They constantly contemplate the virtues of others, being courageous and peerless, with a resolute aspiration for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Their names are as follows:
The Bodhisattva Śailabala, the Bodhisattva Mahāśaila, the Bodhisattva Śailaguhādhara, the Bodhisattva Śailarājasamudgata, the Bodhisattva Śailendrarāja,
the Bodhisattva Mahāvega, the Bodhisattva Śraddhāvega, the Bodhisattva Paravega, the Bodhisattva Priyahasta,
the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, and the Bodhisattva Guṇa...
The Bodhisattva Hastin, the Bodhisattva Dīpāṅguli, the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Nityanikṣiptahasta,
the Bodhisattva Nityapramuditendriya, the Bodhisattva Nityasmṛtimat, the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Nityadarśin,
the Bodhisattva Dharmavīrarāja, the Bodhisattva Vimalaratnaprabhāsa-tejarāja, and Mā...
The Bodhisattva Niprabharāja, the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇapagata, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja,
the Bodhisattva Cittotpādadharmacakrapravartin, the Bodhisattva Dharmavīra, the Bodhisattva Satvaviśodhanaratnavīra,
the Bodhisattva Mārgāṅgarasa, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Asaṅgapratibhāna, and the Bodhisattva Acala.
The Bodhisattva Pādavikrama, the Bodhisattva Vajrapādavikrama, the Bodhisattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva Lakṣaṇavyūhasamudgata, the Bodhisattva Mārajit, the Bodhisattva Jayamati, the Bodhisattva Nāyaka,
the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, and the sixteen great beings including the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla;
The bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, such as Maitreya, led by the fragrance of mandārava flowers from Tuṣita Heaven,
and thirty-two thousand [deities] including the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

Furthermore, all those who are inclined toward the Mahāyāna, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors within this trichiliocosm—the gods of the desire realm, the form realm, and the Pure Abodes—all have assembled to pay homage, make offerings, and prostrate before the Tathāgata!
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma, surrounded with reverence by an immeasurable assembly of hundreds of thousands.

At that moment, seventy-two billion lands away from this buddha-field to the east, there was a buddha-field named Constantly Producing the Sound of the Great Dharma. In that land, there was a Buddha, titled Ratnadanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there.

In this manner, in the Land of Constantly Producing the Great Dharma Sound, all rivers, ponds, springs, and waters; all forests; all various flowers; all leaves; all fruits and blossoms; and all terraces and pavilions constantly produce the unsurpassed sound of the Dharma-treasure.
The sentient beings in that land constantly hear such sublime and wondrous sounds of the Dharma.
This Buddha Ratnadanda constantly emits the great sound of the Dharma; in that land there is a bodhisattva named King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve.

Having beheld the Buddha Ratnadanda, this bodhisattva, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, vanished from that Land of Constantly Emitting Great Dharma Sounds and arrived here in this Sahā world in a single thought-moment.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve manifested eighty-four thousand jeweled terraces, fashioned from exquisite gems. They were perfectly symmetrical in their four sides and four pillars, and their adornments were most sublime. From each individual terrace, he manifested eighty-four thousand jeweled trees, lush with flowers and fruit.
Beneath each tree, he manifested a jeweled lion throne, inlaid with various precious substances, upon which were spread hundreds of thousands of exquisite garments.
Upon all these seats, they saw Buddhas seated, their physical forms, colors, and features identical to those of Śākyamuni!

After the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve had manifested these transformations, he created a jeweled canopy in mid-air, equal in length and breadth to one hundred thousand *yojanas*. It was adorned with hanging silken streamers and networks of bells; when the wind blew through the bell-networks, they produced soft, subtle, lovely, and gentle sounds that resounded throughout the Buddha-world of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
At that time, this trichiliocosm was as level as the palm of a hand, and precious lotus flowers sprang up to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Then, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve, surrounded by eighty-four thousand jeweled terraces, came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the great assembly, having seen this transformation, attained what they had never experienced before and spoke thus:

"According to what we see now, the manner in which this Great Being has come to adorn [this place] indicates that he will surely preach the Great Dharma; furthermore, regarding these various adornments of the trichiliocosm, and moreover, the precious canopy suspended in the air above the Tathāgata, which completely obscures all the celestial palaces."

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:
“Stainless, pure light emerges from the void, Obscuring the splendors of Śakra and Brahmā;
It eclipses the radiance of the sun, moon, jewels, and fire— I pray only that the Honored One among Men explain this sign.”
In this void appears a wondrous jeweled canopy, Pervading and covering hundreds of thousands of yojanas of earth;
Adorned with banners, pennants, bells, and nets— The World-Honored One shall now rain down the Dharma-rain.
The exquisite sounds issued from the nets of bells resound throughout this Buddha-field;
those who hear these sounds find their afflictions stilled—what benefit does he intend to bring by speaking of this?
The three-thousandfold world system is as level as the palm of a hand, and hundreds of thousands of lotuses emerge from the earth;
their fragrance is pleasing and delights both body and mind—by what majestic power has this been wrought?
In the eastern direction, golden light radiates everywhere, With eighty-four thousand exquisite jeweled terraces;
Within the terraces are jeweled trees and lion thrones— Behold them as the Teacher, the Lion of the Śākyas!
O Guide, what beneficial purpose is served by this?
What benefit is gained by seeing this?
What kind of desire is this that you, O Buddha, would know?
"Thus he manifests these immeasurable divine transformations.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"Seventy-two billion buddha-lands to the east of here, there is a land named Constantly Producing the Great Sound of Dharma. Therein dwells a Buddha named Ratnadanda, who is currently present."

There is a bodhisattva there named King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve who has come to this land; having seen me, he prostrated and inquired after the Dharma. For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he has generated a great desire for the Dharma, generated the power of the Dharma, and gathered the wisdom of the Dharma, wishing to manifest all the merits of the Land of Constantly Producing Great Dharma Sounds as well as all the merits of the Buddha Jewel Staff.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve has come to this Sahā world.
In a single day and night, he benefits more sentient beings than all of you great śrāvakas who fill this trichiliocosm could benefit through the Dharma.

Even if you were as numerous as the grains of rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, and forests, and lived for an entire kalpa to benefit sentient beings, you would still not equal [the merit of that person].
The Venerable Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the people of Jambudvīpa were to hear the name of this good man, they would still obtain great benefit; how much more so for those who possess faith and further hear his preaching of the Dharma?”
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve and all the jeweled terraces stood before the Tathāgata and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.

As they paid homage to the Buddha, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; the entire great assembly likewise prostrated at the Tathāgata’s feet.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve circumambulated the Buddha three times; together with eighty-four thousand jeweled towers, they also circumambulated him three times. Having completed the three circumambulations, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and praised him in verse:
“Your speech is skillfully gentle, subtle, and wondrous, Unerring, unmixed, pure, and stainless;
With a good name, majestic virtue, and wisdom supreme among the wise, I now bow my head to you, the most excellent Sage.”
Fulfilling hundreds of thousands of billions of merits, you bestow peace and happiness to extinguish a hundred sufferings;
with benevolence, great compassion, and joy equal toward the three realms, you expound the Dharma to remove all defilements.
The Buddhas of the ten directions praise your benevolent virtue: That you have attained Bodhi during this evil age;
That you deliver suffering sentient beings without weariness— For it is difficult to deliver even a single sentient being.
All Buddhas are entirely equal; their wisdom and penetrating power are identical, and they are honored as the Foremost among Men.
Having attained the peerless, pure, and white Dharma, they manifest in humble and inferior forms to discipline sentient beings.
If the World-Honored One were to reveal the entire realm of the Buddha, all sentient beings would have their minds confounded and distracted;
therefore, out of great compassion for the sake of benefiting them, he practices what they should practice and expounds the Dharma.
The Honored among Men, supreme in wisdom, beloved by all; always first with a gentle countenance and soft speech;
his merit as reckoned among humans and devas is peerless—therefore, with joy, I prostrate before the Honored One!
The Omniscient One who tames all sentient beings, Who exhausts all dharmas and subdues the heterodox;
The Omniscient One whose vision overcomes the demonic enemies— I bow my head to the One of a hundred powers who subdues all powers.
Always delighting in speech that is true and sincere, Well-knowing how to act as one speaks;
Unshakable by suffering or joy, like the king of mountains— I now bow my head to you who bestow worldly happiness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve, having praised the Buddha with verses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Tathāgata Ratnadaṇḍa inquires after the World-Honored One’s health:”
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy, and do you dwell in peace and happiness?
"World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a few questions of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. If the Buddha would grant me leave, I would venture to consult you."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Infinite Resolve: “Good son!
The Tathāgata always grants permission; whatever doubts you may have, ask freely as you wish. I shall, in accordance with your questions, expound the teaching that will gladden your heart.”
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard from former Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that there is a teaching called the ‘Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury.

If a bodhisattva dwells in this treasury, they will attain the inexhaustible Dharma and attain inexhaustible eloquence; they will behold the inexhaustibility of the Buddhas and be well able to obtain inexhaustible supernormal powers, serving as a true refuge for all sentient beings.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound for us the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Infinite Resolve:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
you are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a Dharma.”
"Good son! You have already planted various roots of goodness and inquired of [the Dharma] under as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. Good son!"
"Listen now attentively and reflect well upon it!
I shall briefly explain the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury.
The Bodhisattva King Adorned with Infinite Resolve then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, Blessed One," he replied,
and having received the instruction, he listened.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury refers to the mind of omniscience."

Having generated this mind, one guards it firmly, neither regressing nor abandoning it, remaining undisturbed. One maintains excellent mindfulness, ardently exhorts others, and provides instruction and admonition. With roots of goodness as the foremost priority, one joyfully guards them and constantly and steadfastly performs the deeds that ought to be done: for the sake of generosity, for the sake of ethical discipline, for the sake of patience, for the sake of diligence, for the sake of meditative concentration, and for the sake of skillful means.

This mind serves as a pillar; it is neither timid nor weak, neither frail nor broken, free from indolence, and neither turning away nor abandoning; one should accord with this mind and awaken to its realization.
With wholesome karma as the foremost, one is upright and without crookedness, dwelling correctly in rectitude, free from illusion and deceit;

having acted, one has no regrets, and regarding what has not yet been done, one acts upon it, diligently practicing what ought to be practiced, abandoning unwholesome conduct and diligently cultivating right conduct.
"Noble son!
This is called the Dharma-gate for entering the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
It is the firm resolve for omniscience, which one should cherish, firmly guard, and never abandon."
“Good son! What is the firmness of the mind of omniscience? Good son!”
There are four ways in which the mind of omniscience is firm. What are these four?
Not thinking of other vehicles, not prostrating to other deities, not giving rise to other thoughts, and having an unswerving resolve.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"Do not give rise to thoughts of other vehicles; Pay homage to the Buddha, but do not pay homage to devas."
One does not give rise to other sensual desires, nor does one pay homage to external worldlings.
When practicing this Dharma, the mind of omniscience is firm;
neither Māra nor external paths can find even a hair’s breadth of an opening.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are four dharmas that protect the mind of omniscience.
What are these four?
"One is not intoxicated by form or by wealth and possessions; one is not intoxicated by kin or by power.
These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"One is not intoxicated by wealth, property, or rank, nor by kin or sovereignty;
rather, one remains heedful regarding wealth, property, rank, sovereignty, and kin.
Observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), one sees that they are entirely impermanent."
"Through heedfulness and freedom from pride, one guards the bodhicitta.
By practicing these meritorious dharmas, one proceeds toward enlightenment without regression.
This first verse constitutes the "half-verse on practice. "Good son!"
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one does not regress from the bodhicitta.
What are these four?

Accumulating all the pāramitās; associating with true bodhisattvas; cultivating and accumulating the mind of great compassion; and gathering all sentient beings through the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu).
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"Constantly practicing the six perfections without satiety, Born of learning, and having heard them, the mind becomes supple."
Born with great aspiration and free from evil friends, One draws near to virtuous friends according to one's needs.
Constantly cultivating the supreme path and approaching those who have realized it, Always practicing compassion and abiding in the four means of integration;
Always delighting in firmly abiding in the bodhicitta— Then the accumulation of the Buddha’s qualities will not be difficult to attain.
“Good son! A bodhisattva who is endowed with four dharmas does not abandon the mind of omniscience.
What are these four?
"Faith in the Buddha’s merit, cultivating and gathering the Buddha’s wisdom, beholding the Buddha’s supernormal powers, and not severing the lineage of the Buddhas—
these are called the four.
Then he spoke in verse:
Having gained faith and understanding in the Buddha’s virtues, one diligently cultivates and accumulates the Buddha’s wisdom;
having witnessed the Buddha’s supernormal powers, one diligently protects the lineage of the Buddhas.
Practicing such dharmas, one does not abandon the bodhicitta.
"According to the various Buddhas he beholds, his power of diligence increases all the more. 'Good son!
When a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, he will never disturb or confuse the mind of enlightenment.'"
What are the four?
To attend upon the presence of the Buddhas; to hear the Dharma from the Tathāgatas; to constantly extol the virtues of the Buddha; and to rely on tranquility while mindfully recollecting the Buddha.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"To serve the Tathāgata!"
One should be respectful and reverent;
whatever Dharma one hears, having heard it, one should practice according to the teaching.
Constantly praise the Tathāgata!
They believe in, revere, and delight in it;
having heard the sublime Dharma directly from the face [of the Teacher], the wise rely upon its meaning.
They constantly praise his virtues, he who is the Tamer of all that exists in the world.
He always diligently relies upon them, maintaining right mindfulness toward all Buddhas.
Repeatedly praising the virtues of the Buddhas, he constantly and diligently observes his own conduct;
always delighting in solitary and quiet places, he contemplates the Tathāgata.
“Skillfully upholding such dharmas, practicing with an undistracted mind—
such a person possesses samādhi and does not forget the bodhicitta. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, they will remember the bodhicitta.
What are these four?
"I must become a field of merit for all sentient beings; I shall proclaim the path; I shall follow the course taken by the Tathāgatas; and I shall truly know the conduct of all sentient beings."
"These are the four.
Then he spoke in verse:
"I shall become a supreme field of merit for the world, showing the correct path to those who have entered onto deviant ways."
Wherever the Sugata goes, there I shall go; I shall always know the conduct of sentient beings.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates these virtues, they constantly maintain the mind set upon the supreme path of Bodhi.
Such a one shall swiftly become a Dharma King, attaining supernatural powers and wisdom peerless in the world.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, he maintains the mind of omniscience.
What are these four?

To focus one's will and mindfulness is the foundation of all dharmas; one should be mindful of this foundation of dharmas. To give rise to the mind of omniscience is a world-treasure stupa; one should be mindful of this treasure stupa.
These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"One should focus the mind with single-minded intent; One should maintain this excellent, focused mindfulness.
This is the foundation of all dharmas, The stupa for the entire world."
“Constantly mindful of the bodhicitta, dwelling with a mind that delights in abiding well—this is the root of the Ten Powers;
it shall be a stūpa for gods and the world.
“O son of good family!”
When a bodhisattva is endowed with four qualities, they kindle the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
What are these four? They are:

gathering power and supernormal faculties without losing their original practice; fulfilling the strength of the five faculties; exerting physical and mental vigor while remaining free from the notion of a self; and practicing diligence with assiduity for the benefit of others.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"The four dharmas that have been expounded kindle the bodhicitta."
If one’s wisdom is blazing, one attains the cessation of afflictions;
through power and penetration, one thus exerts diligent effort.
Having donned these and abiding therein, one is adorned and free from indolence.
Thus not failing one's original vow, one dwells securely in the faculties and powers;
with body and mind free from weariness, one diligently strives to seek the true body.
Abiding thus in fervent zeal, one increases the bodhicitta.
His wisdom is thus, increasing like the sun and the moon.
"Good son, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva encourages the bodhicitta."
What are the four? They are:

praising and extolling the bodhicitta in the midst of the great assembly; causing others to understand and resolve upon the bodhicitta; properly receiving instruction and following one's teachers to give rise to a pure mind; and ensuring that all afflictions do not gain mastery over them.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"To exhort others and sing of the mind of the Way, one must first abide in this as the foundation."
When one possesses all-knowledge, one is called a knower of causes.
This mind of all-knowledge is pure and ever-illuminating;
abiding eternally within it, one is venerated by the world.
Constantly uttering gentle speech, swiftly receiving instruction and admonition;
inquiring of teachers and elders regarding the supreme mind of omniscience;
with a nature that is eternally pure, one protects the bodhicitta.
Pure and free from afflictions, most excellent and without contradiction.
"Good son! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva manifests the bodhicitta."
What are the four?

This is my dwelling place; having dwelt in this place, I have revealed and expounded [the Dharma]; I know that within this mind there are immeasurable virtues; and I also speak of such matters to others.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"Well-established in that which is to be established, the Bodhisattva dwells having attained this."
Praising such a Dharma, the wondrous mind of Bodhi—
The virtue of the bodhicitta is immeasurable, whether in its arousal or its praise;
Having praised it, one then acts accordingly, Attaining that which the praiser obtains.
“Good son! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva teaches the cultivation of the bodhicitta.
What are these four?
That is to say: one is not coarse or violent; one’s speech is gentle; one is free from harshness; and one’s countenance is harmonious and pleasant.
These are the four. Then he spoke a verse:
“Explaining the meaning with gentleness, always free from harshness;
dwelling in this Dharma with a serene countenance—this is the teaching on the bodhicitta. ‘Good son!
Bodhisattvas possess four dharmas, with the roots of goodness of the bodhicitta as their foremost.
What are these four?

To fulfill the primary and secondary marks by opening wide the gates of great giving; to cultivate pure buddha-fields by practicing various forms of generosity; to purify wisdom by constantly subduing arrogance; and to satisfy wisdom by cultivating and accumulating extensive learning.
"These are called the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"Always keeping the gates open and practicing great giving, one reaches the shore of the marks and signs of excellence."
Skillfully bestowing various kinds of gifts, one shall possess a pure land;
always free from arrogance, constantly seeking to accumulate the Buddha’s wisdom;
never being satiated in gathering learning—one possesses sharp and beneficial wisdom.
Such supreme and wondrous marks arise through skillful means as the roots of the Path;
they are turned by a skillful mind that gathers all prior merits.
"O son of good family!
Bodhisattvas have four qualities through which they always experience joy and delight.
What are these four? They are:
delighting in seeing the Buddha.
Seeing other bodhisattvas who possess superior diligence, they give rise to joy and happiness, saying:
"When shall I fulfill the requirements to receive the prediction [of enlightenment]?
Thus they receive the prediction for the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
"When shall I perform the deeds of a Buddha before all sentient beings?
Thus one gives rise to a mind of joy and delight toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"When shall I behold the Buddha face-to-face?
Thus, he gave rise to joy and delight, desiring to see the Buddha.
Seeing other bodhisattvas who have attained superior progress, one gives rise to joy and desires to practice this diligence:
"When shall I fulfill the accumulation of merit?
When shall I receive the supreme prediction and realize awakening?"
When shall I become a Dharma King in a certain direction through supreme wisdom? May the Bodhisattva always give rise to such joyful aspiration:
"At what time in the world shall I perform the work of a Buddha, attain the wisdom of supernormal powers, and reach the other shore?"
"With fame spreading throughout the ten directions and receiving offerings, the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to this joyful desire.
'Good son! There are four things that the Bodhisattva does not delight in.'"
What are the four? They are:
not delighting in praising unreal merits or obtaining various gains and offerings;
and not delighting in obtaining the wealth and pleasures of Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, and devas.
He does not delight in any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
he does not delight in any superior offerings received by followers of external paths.
These are the four things in which he does not delight.
And he spoke in verse:
"I take no pleasure in fame, great profit, or offerings; I am likewise indifferent toward body, life, or wealth!
I take no pleasure in Śakra, Brahmā, or the World-Protectors; All these false existences are entirely impermanent."
They take no delight in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, except for those who have resolved upon the superior vehicle;
they take no delight in worldly dhyānas or those of non-Buddhists, nor do they take delight in the view of a self or the view of extremes.
“Good son! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva protects the mind of omniscience.
What are the four?

To speak according to how things are, to speak according to how one abides, to speak according to how one acts, and to have a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings while generating an intense aspiration for wholesome dharmas—
these are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
“As it is taught, as it is abided, and as it is practiced— With an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, one seeks the path intensely;
Abiding well in these four supreme dharmas, One always protects the bodhicitta so as not to forget or lose it.”
“Good son! There are four dharmas that a bodhisattva ought to practice.
What are these four?
"Cultivating and accumulating much learning, reflecting upon what has been heard, explaining what has been heard, and not regressing from tranquility—
these are the four.
Then he spoke in verse:
"This one constantly and diligently gathers what has not yet been heard; this one constantly cultivates mindfulness and reflection upon what has been heard much;
this one constantly and diligently speaks of what has been heard much; this one constantly and diligently practices for the sake of attaining dhyāna."
“Good son! A bodhisattva possesses two dharmas by which they practice giving while remaining fixed in the mind of omniscience.
What are these two?
Single-mindedly focusing the mind on meditative concentration;
and equanimity, without hoping for karmic retribution—
these are the two.
And he spoke in verse:
“Giving with a joyful heart, Having given, one feels joy and expects no reward;
Relinquishing everything for the sake of enlightenment, One realizes enlightenment through giving with a concentrated mind.”
“Good son! There are two dharmas by which a bodhisattva, with omniscience as the foremost, practices and maintains pure precepts.
What are these two?
"To have no intent to harm toward any sentient beings, and to give rise to great compassion for those who violate the precepts—
these are the two.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Without giving rise to thoughts of malice or harm, one bestows gifts equally upon those who are superior, middling, or inferior;
and one further increases the cultivation of compassion toward sentient beings who are wicked and rebellious. Good son!"
Bodhisattvas possess two dharmas through which they practice patience, taking omniscience as their primary goal.
What are these two? They are:
relinquishing one's own happiness and bestowing happiness upon others.
"These are the two.
And he spoke in verse:
"Seeking no pleasure for oneself, one always acts for the benefit and happiness of others."
Possessing such patience as this, one takes the awakening of a Buddha (*buddhabodhi*) as the path. "Good son!
A bodhisattva has two dharmas through which they practice diligence, with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as the foremost."
What are the two?
Taking the bodhicitta as foremost and not abandoning all sentient beings—
these are the two.
And he spoke in verse:
"Practicing all that is pure and white, With the mind of the supreme path as the foremost;
Seeing neither self nor sentient beings, One's diligence remains undiminished."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes two dharmas, he practices meditative concentration with omniscience as the foremost.
What are these two?
"Entering meditative concentration through skillful means and emerging through the power of original vows—
these are the two.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The courageous and steadfast always arise; the wise practice meditative concentration.
Having subdued all fetters and afflictions, they constantly desire to attain dhyāna.
Sustained by the power of their original vows, they shall become guides for the world."
Possessing such virtues as these, one attains meditative concentration. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes two dharmas, they possess wisdom that takes omniscience as its foremost priority."
What are the two?
First, to be personally free from all views; second, to cultivate wisdom for the sake of severing the views of all sentient beings.
These are the two.
And he spoke in verse:
"He is free from all views, Cultivating benefit for sentient beings;
With supreme wisdom manifest before him, He proceeds upon the path with wisdom and peace."
“Good son! A bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas possesses skillful means.
What are these four?

Out of compassion for sentient beings, he acts as their savior; his great compassion is genuine and free from weariness; because he delights in the Dharma, he gives rise to joy; and having abandoned all afflictions, he is without any timidity.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"Cultivate loving-kindness without anger; give rise to compassion without weariness."
"By means of the Dharma one gives rise to joy, and abandons afflictions without difficulty.
'Good son! A bodhisattva has four things that never weary."
What are the four? They are:
insatiability in hearing the Dharma, lack of satiety in accumulating merit, lack of satiety in dwelling in forest retreats, and lack of satiety in dedication.
These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"In seeking learning there is no satiety; likewise, one who accumulates merit finds no satiety. In dwelling in forest hermitages there is no satiety;
in dedicating merit there is no satiety. Thus, for a bodhisattva, these four things are never wearied."
“Good son! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is never satisfied.
What are these four?
This bodhisattva, recollecting the past buddhas, forms this thought:
"All these buddhas fully cultivated and accumulated supreme enlightenment; why should I not now likewise cultivate and accumulate it?"
He reflects on the Buddhas of the future, thinking:
"I, too, shall be included among their number.
He reflects on the Buddhas of the present, and while reflecting upon them, he forms this thought:
"These Buddhas and others fully perceive and understand all dharmas.
Within these recollections, there is no timidity or weakness.
This is the fourth.
And he spoke in verse:
"Recalling the Buddhas of the past, my fearlessness increases;
Since those Buddhas attained the supreme path, why should I not attain it as well?"
Reflecting on the Sugatas of the future, I am among their number;
with no timidity and redoubled diligence, I shall certainly be among their number.
Reflecting on the present Teacher when he was practicing the bodhisattva path:
I shall eliminate all fetters and realize the nirvana of bodhi.
Understanding all phenomena, I shall abide as I desire;
never shall I give rise to a timid heart, but instead generate a twofold zeal for superior progress.
“Good son! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not regress from the Mahāyāna.
What are the four?
"Their mind is like the earth; their mind is like water; their mind is like fire; their mind is like wind.
These are the four.
Then he spoke in verse:
"His mind is like earth and water; his mind is also like wind and fire.
Whether he acts or does not act, he is equal; he shall attain the Way and never regress. "Good son!
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva understands and realizes non-self.
What are these four?
This bodhisattva forms the following thought:
"I shall fully know the mental activities of all realms of sentient beings.
"I shall fully know the faculties of all realms of sentient beings and preach the Dharma accordingly."

“I shall sever all afflictions for the sake of all realms of sentient beings and preach the Dharma for them; we have awakened to the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas. Truly, it is not my body that can awaken to this Dharma, nor is it my mind.”
“I am able to awaken to this Dharma through my various roots of goodness; one who is without a self is called a bodhisattva!
These are the four.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The minds of all sentient beings, and their activities, are inconceivable;
through afflictions and false discrimination, deluded thoughts give rise to right and wrong.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise thus—immeasurable and inconceivable.”
This is not within my power to fully comprehend the Buddha’s wisdom.
It is contrary to all fetters and afflictions; formless and invisible, I shall utterly sever it all and reveal the path to liberation.
“Good son! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is free from timidity.
What are these four?
"I vow that all roots of goodness shall cultivate skillful wisdom, cultivate the powers of faith, diligence, and mindfulness, and have faith in the unsurpassed path.
These are the four.
Then he spoke in verse:
“With wholesome joy and fullness, with the many fragrances of wisdom and skillful means;
with faith, diligence, mindfulness, and power—therein lies the path to liberation.
These four dharmas of wisdom, one upholds them without weariness.”
A refuge for those who are weary, and a savior for the world.

“Good son! There are four obstructive dharmas that a bodhisattva should recognize. What are the four?
Slandering the true Dharma, being stingy and withholding the Dharma, harboring overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and practicing the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*).”
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"The bodhicitta has four [aspects]; they are taught and shown as obstacles."
A bodhisattva should recognize these and repeatedly distance himself from them:
slandering the true Dharma; being stingy with what one has heard much;
arrogance and pride; and giving rise to meditative concentration through unwholesome means.
Therefore, protect the True Dharma; having heard it, disseminate it widely.
Abandon arrogance and pride, and remain far removed from those who lack meditative concentration.
"O son of good family!
Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which their undertakings are swift.
What are these four?
Their actions are performed with wisdom and not with pride;
All roots of goodness are dedicated toward Bodhi and do not incline toward the Lesser Vehicle;
one does not give rise to defiled attachment toward any of the realms of existence, and if such attachment should arise, it is solely for the purpose of transforming sentient beings;
throughout the three periods of day and night, one constantly practices the three divisions [of the day] to extinguish past evil karma and refrain from creating it in the future.
"These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"What is performed is done with wisdom, not with pride; Dedicating merit toward the Supreme Path, not the Lesser Vehicle."
The wise do not place faith in any form of existence, but resolve their minds to benefit all sentient beings.
Three times during the day and likewise at night,
they repent three times to extinguish their prior evils.
Not committing various evils and accumulating all virtues—thus does the wise person accumulate wholesome karma.
"Good son! There are four dharmas that are most excellent for a bodhisattva."
What are the four?
Not praising oneself, not disparaging others, staying far removed from all evils, and abandoning all forms of pride.
These are the four.
And he spoke in verse:
"One does not praise oneself nor disparage others; one repents all evils committed and vows not to do them again;
one gives rise to neither pride nor arrogance, but with a mind upright and straight, cultivates virtuous conduct."
“Good son! There are two dharmas by which a bodhisattva is upright and swift.
What are these two?
"If one answers as it truly is whatever is asked, and does not conceal anything previously seen—
this is the second.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Explaining in accordance with what is asked, without concealing what one has previously perceived;
rather than sacrificing body or life, one would never speak a falsehood.
To be upright in this Dharma is the root of noble virtue."
He attains straightforwardness and swiftly awakens to supreme enlightenment.
"Good son! A bodhisattva has two qualities by which there is no flattery or deceit."
What are the two?
Although one gains much profit, one does not wish to praise one's own virtues; when one receives no offerings or support, one does not exalt oneself.
These are the two.
And he spoke in verse:
"Though one may gain much profit and support, one does not praise or display one's own virtues;
this is what those of great wisdom do not desire, and it is attained by those who are not deceitful."
"If one does not obtain gain or offerings, this is my original vocation;
I do not wish for others to fall into error, nor do I wish to cause their karma to ripen.
"O son of good family!"
A bodhisattva possesses two qualities by which they do not expect recompense from others.
What are these two?
"I ought to benefit all sentient beings; it is not that sentient beings should benefit me."
"I shall awaken to it and realize it as Bodhi.
This is the second.
Then he spoke in verse:
"I shall benefit sentient beings; I bear their burdens.
I seek the path of the unconditioned, without looking for recompense from others.
I do not seek the conditioned; I seek the path of the unconditioned."
"I protect and sustain the world, yet I do not hope for recompense in order to attain the Way.
Good son! A bodhisattva has two dharmas by which they perform what ought not to be done."
What are the two?
To constantly provide for those who do not recognize one's kindness, and to entrust heavy responsibilities to those who do recognize one's kindness.
These are the two.
And he spoke in verse:
"To sentient beings who do not recognize kindness, I expect no recompense from them;
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases— All are made into bodhi."
“Good son! There are two dharmas in which a bodhisattva should abide.
What are these two?
"Constantly encountering the Buddhas and also constantly meeting those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle—
these are the two.
Then he spoke in verse:
"In two kinds of places one should dwell; in such places, one's reputation increases.
One shall encounter all Tathāgatas—this is what Bodhisattvas recognize.
O son of good family!"
There are two things that a bodhisattva should not practice.
What are these two?
Not dwelling together with those who have made no vow to practice the Śrāvaka vehicle; and...
"Not being startled or afraid of the various realms of existence, and dwelling alone in quietude and silence— these are the two.
Then he spoke in verse:
"One does not dwell together with those who do not practice;
one is not terrified by the various realms of existence, but relies upon the place of tranquil seclusion.
O son of good family!"
This is called the fundamental phrase for first entering the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
If a bodhisattva enters this initial fundamental phrase, that bodhisattva will be able to accomplish the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.

When the World-Honored One spoke these initial verses on entering the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, sixty thousand sentient beings—both devas and humans—aroused the mind set on unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment; ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas; and five hundred bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any dharmas, forever exhausted all outflows, and their minds attained liberation.

At that time, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways and a great light shone everywhere. The musical instruments of humans and devas resounded spontaneously without being struck. Humans, devas, asuras, and others raised their voices in unison, chanting three times these words:

"Any sentient beings who hear this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury will swiftly obtain excellent benefit. If there are those who write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to its teaching, such beings shall all never lose this secret treasury of the Tathāgata."
At that time, having heard this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve thought to himself:
"By what kind of offerings should I now worship the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
He further thought:
"External objects are easy to relinquish, but internal matters are difficult to relinquish; I should now offer my own body as a gift to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One!"
He immediately ascended into the air and spoke these verses:
"I now serve the Pratyekabuddha, Making this very body my offering;
By means of this unsurpassed renunciation, I vow that you shall become like the Teacher."
To offer material wealth to the Two-legged Honored One is not difficult;
what, then, is rare?
It is that which is called bodily offering.
"I now make offering to the Peerless One; with my own body, I pay homage to the All-Seeing One.
To become an object of worship for the world of humans and devas, I am like a lion of great wisdom.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve cast his body down upon the Tathāgata.

At that time, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, unprecedented flowers—extraordinary in kind and color, exceedingly fresh, pure, and most exquisitely beautiful—were scattered over the Tathāgata.

This bodhisattva’s body neither fell to the ground nor appeared in the air; these various flowers reached the Buddha’s body and then immediately leaped back up, remaining suspended in mid-air to form a great flower canopy that covered the four continents.

From within these flower canopies, flower garlands hang down, emitting great radiance; within this radiance appear wondrous lotus flowers, upon which sit bodhisattvas, such as the King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve.
These bodhisattvas rose from their lotus pedestals, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with one voice made this request:

“We pray only that the World-Honored One will expound the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury so that it shall not be severed, and that he will protect the retinue of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.”
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa gave rise to a sense of wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve has made an offering to the Tathāgata by adorning his own body; having thus offered his body to the Tathāgata, he now manifests these various displays of the Bodhisattva’s adornments.”
World-Honored One!
May all sentient beings alike attain such a body adorned with these marks; may the Tathāgata remain in the world for a constant lifespan.
World-Honored One!
"We have now truly attained great benefit, for we have been able to see this virtuous Great Being and hear his preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa,
"Do you now see this Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve?"
“I have seen them, World-Honored One! “Kāśyapa!
These are good sons!”
In the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you have constantly requested this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury;
likewise, in the presence of all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall also inquire about this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound upon this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, as requested by these bodhisattvas!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"Listen well now!
This is a small portion of the Dharma from the Tathāgata’s secret treasury."
"Why is this? If one were to expound this Dharma for an entire kalpa, it could not be exhausted.
Kāśyapa said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, Kāśyapa and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"Kāśyapa, what do you think?"

You may think that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, all those sentient beings who repeatedly caused me distress—by whom I gave away my hands, feet, head, eyes, ears, nose, skin, flesh, bones, marrow, blood, and even my wife and children, and briefly stated, all my wealth and possessions—did not fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or other evil destinies. [In fact, they did.]

Why is this? Because when he was originally a bodhisattva, his resolve was pure; because of his great vows and his accumulation of pure precepts; and because his great compassion toward all sentient beings was utterly sincere and steadfastly enduring.

Because of great compassion; because of the dharma of great merit; because of firm and powerful diligence directed toward the Great Vehicle; because of the purity of one's own mind; because of the abundance of great vows; and because of not delighting in one's own pleasure.
If there are sentient beings who provoke, harass, revile, or abuse a bodhisattva, by virtue of that bodhisattva’s merit, they shall not fall into the evil destinies. Kāśyapa,
I shall now provide an analogy to clarify this meaning.
Kāśyapa!
It is just as when a sick person is given medicine by a skilled physician, yet that patient reviles both the medicine and the physician; having first reviled them, he subsequently takes the medicine.
Kāśyapa! What do you think?
Does medicine cease to be medicine simply because it is reviled?
“Is your illness not yet cured? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Even if one reviles and scolds it, it does not lose its medicinal potency and is still able to eliminate the illness.

In this same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva is like that medicine and the skilled physician; although they may not be respected and may encounter various forms of provocation, the bodhisattva’s pure and resolute intention remains entirely without deficiency."
Kāśyapa!
It is like a great precious gem composed of manifold virtues, its nature being pure and free from all blemishes.
Yet, there may be humans or devas who revile and abuse this jewel, failing to show it respect.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Does this great precious gem lose its jewel-like power because it fears being reviled or insulted?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! This pure jewel is like that bodhisattva whose resolve is pure: even if all sentient beings do not show them respect, their merits suffer no diminution.”
“Kāśyapa!
Suppose there were a great oil lamp; even if humans or devas were to revile and abuse it, would it become dark because of that reviling and abuse? “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”
The bodhisattva’s resolve is pure in this way; even when provoked or troubled, they do not lose their nature.
Kāśyapa, for this reason you should know that although there may be those who provoke or harass a bodhisattva, such beings do not fall into the evil realms.
"Why is this? It is because the original vows of these bodhisattvas are pure; thus, all their aspirations are fulfilled.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!

According to my understanding of the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, if one gives rise to unwholesome karma toward the Tathāgata, will such sentient beings likewise not fear falling into the evil realms?”
The Buddha said: “It is so, Kāśyapa!

If there are sentient beings who give rise to a mind of faith and reverence toward the Tathāgata of Great Compassion, understanding, entering, and progressing [toward him], whether while the Buddha is present or after his parinirvāṇa—if they offer to the Tathāgata or his stūpa banners, pennants, canopies, flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, jewels, robes, or various kinds of food and drink, according to whatever various things they possess;”
Whether taking or eating, whether taking it oneself or instructing another to take it— Kāśyapa,
I say that such a person has committed no offense. Kāśyapa!

Poverty is the greatest suffering because it leads to a lack of respect, to acts of robbery, to fearlessness, to a lack of faith and reverence, to a failure to understand karma, to a disregard for retribution, to greedy seeking, to being difficult to subdue, to the presence of greed, hatred, and delusion, and to a lack of shame and remorse; and because of its cruelty and wickedness, one does not contemplate that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, nor does one believe that the Tathāgata brings vast benefit to sentient beings. If one takes even a single thread from a stūpa of the Tathāgata—whether taking it oneself or causing another to take it—I declare that such a person has committed no small offense, and I do not say that they will not fall into the evil realms.
Kāśyapa!

If there are sentient beings who, regarding the property of the Tathāgata or the property of a stūpa, either take it themselves or incite others to take it—the Tathāgata now fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, by means of this very condition, they shall attain the severance of their fetters.
Why is this? Because the mental conduct of such a person is protected by the Buddha. Kāśyapa!
If one directs the mind toward the Tathāgata or a stūpa of the Tathāgata, even giving rise to a slight sense of remorse, Kāśyapa!

that sentient being’s mind will naturally undergo repentance; because they have given rise to a remorseful mind by taking the Tathāgata as their object, they turn away from all the sins of saṃsāra, and their fetters and afflictions become subtly relaxed.
Kāśyapa! Suppose there were a person or a celestial being who fell to the earth; having fallen to the great earth, they would rely upon that very earth to rise and stand again.
It is just so, Kāśyapa!

Because these sentient beings give rise to unwholesome thoughts toward the Tathāgata, they fall into the evil realms; yet once they have fallen into the evil realms, by again taking the Tathāgata as their object of focus, they quickly attain liberation.
"What is meant by 'taking the Tathāgata as one's object' and 'generating a mind of profound reverence toward the Tathāgata'?
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!

If even a person with such a wicked and thieving mind can obtain great benefit by giving rise to a thought that takes the Tathāgata as their object of mindfulness, how much more so for one with a pure mind?”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa! As you have said,

if there are sentient beings who give rise to thoughts of the Tathāgata, recollect the Tathāgata, or contemplate the conditions of the Tathāgata, all such individuals shall attain the realization of the fruit of nirvāṇa.”
“Venerable Sir!
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it would be better to commit unwholesome karma against the Tathāgata than to offer worship to those who hold the wrong views of external paths.
Why is this? If the Tathāgata were to give rise to unwholesome karma, he would necessarily feel regret, and ultimately he would surely attain nirvāṇa;
however, by following the views of non-Buddhists, one would fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
The Buddha said,
“Kāśyapa, it is as you have said.”
Kāśyapa! Suppose there were a person among gods or humans who reviled red sandalwood, striking it with their hands and quickly tossing it to the ground. Kāśyapa!
"What do you think?
What kind of fragrance does such a person have?
Kāśyapa replied:
"And this person possesses the fragrance of sandalwood.
"In the same way, Kāśyapa,

if there are sentient beings who see the Tathāgata with their eyes, hear him with their ears, or proclaim his name with their mouths, you should know that these people possess the fragrance of liberation."
Kāśyapa!

Suppose there were a person who, having taken hold of excrement and filth, were to offer it worship with various musical instruments and all kinds of flowers; what kind of fragrance would such a person have?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This person possesses nothing but excrement, filth, and foul stench.”
“In this way, Kāśyapa!
You should know that those who associate with, revere, and make offerings to various non-Buddhists are likewise in this regard:
they possess the fear of various views, and the fear of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.”

Kāśyapa! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family has faith that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion; if they venerate and believe with earnestness, eliminating pride and arrogance; if they are free from greed, hatred, and delusion; if their resolve is firm and they understand the retribution of karma; if they are upright, without flattery or deceit; and if they have attained pure faith in the Tathāgata—with their faculties free from greed and crookedness, their will unshakable, and pure faith perfected—they believe in the Buddha’s great compassion which benefits many sentient beings, they believe in the Buddha’s past practices and in the Tathāgata himself, and they do not abandon any sentient beings whatsoever.

He has such a mind and such an intention: "Even if I lack food, medicine, or other necessities, as long as I have not yet attained the fruits of the Way nor entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma), if I obtain these necessities, I shall be able to attain the fruits of the Way and enter the stage of certainty; if I do not obtain them, I will become emaciated by hunger and thirst and will be unable to cultivate goodness or attain the fruits of the Way."
If such a person takes for themselves the property of the Tathāgata— whether robes, food and drink, or medicines required for illness—
and consumes them, Kāśyapa,
I do not say that they will suffer the retribution of the evil realms.
Kāśyapa! This is called the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.

You should maintain it in secrecy and guard it well; you must not reveal or expound it before those who are attached to their own views, lest such persons further increase the weight of their dogmatic perspectives.

"What is bondage? Kāśyapa,
that which is called bondage is attachment."
What is meant by "understanding"?
It is non-attachment and not discriminating between duality. Kāśyapa!
I do not say that one who is free from attachment commits an offense.
Why is this? Kāśyapa!
Weak and inferior afflictions arise from falsehood.
Kāśyapa, because they are unreal and do not truly arise, they are called "real."
Kāśyapa! I now cite a metaphor to demonstrate the nature of unreal, false conceptualization. Kāśyapa!
It is just as when a person or a deity takes a fire made from a mustard seed and blows upon it to make it grow, gradually burning various objects until it becomes a great mass of fire.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, foolish ordinary people give rise to a small amount of improper reflection and deluded thoughts; they cling firmly to various views and follow their own false imaginings, whereby their fetters increase in all those places.
Kāśyapa! Suppose there were a mass of fire as large as Mount Sumeru that had no basis for support. Kāśyapa!
"What do you think?
Will this fire increase, or will it gradually be extinguished?
Kāśyapa replied:
"This fire shall now be extinguished and shall no longer increase.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"

If unreal imaginings, the various afflictions, and so forth do not arise again, and if one no longer clings to them, no longer imagines them, no longer delights in them, and no longer discriminates them, these shall gradually cease and not increase.
Kāśyapa! For this reason, you should understand that these weak, unsubstantial, false conceptualizations and afflictions are not real. Kāśyapa!
It is like a person who has gone to a house containing poison, yet without actually consuming it, becomes terrified in his heart and suffers great pain, crying out loudly:
"I have encountered poison! I have encountered poison!"
"Suppose there were a skilled physician who, possessing an unreal medicine, caused this patient to eliminate that unreal illness and become free from all suffering.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?"
“If a skilled physician were to provide this person with the actual medicine, would this person live? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"This person did not actually consume poison, yet he conceived the notion that he had; therefore, an unreal medicine must be used to treat him.
The Buddha said, "It is even so, Kāśyapa!"
"Because all ordinary worldlings are afflicted by unreal defilements, the Tathāgata speaks of unreal dharmas.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma not accord with reality?
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”
"What you have explained— is it true or is it not true?
Kāśyapa replied, "What I have explained is not true."
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
All greed is countered by the contemplation of impurity; hatred is countered by loving-kindness; and delusion is countered by the contemplation of causes and conditions.
World-Honored One!
If impurity were real, it could not eliminate unreal lust; nor would lust give rise to the contemplation of impurity.
If delusion were real, once delusion had arisen, it would not be countered by causes and conditions, nor could causes and conditions eliminate delusion.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
Both all the fetters and the dharmas for severing the fetters are both unreal; they are without substance, without fixedness, and without accomplishment.
Therefore, these unreal afflictions and the like, by associating with what is unreal, are eliminated.
World-Honored One!
The fetters have no going away.
Why is this? If there is the removal [of going], then there is going; if there is already going, then there is coming.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
"All fetters and afflictions neither come nor go; therefore, know that all conditioned phenomena neither come nor go—this is called being free from affliction.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
"This secret treasury of the Tathāgata teaches that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Are these ten paths of unwholesome action, as taught by the Buddha, by nature stainless and pure in their fundamental nature?
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is.”
Kāśyapa! Why is this?
There is no one who possesses sovereign power who would commit the act of killing.
One does not commit theft out of a lack of trustworthiness;
one does not commit sexual misconduct toward that which is ownerless or unprotected;
and one does not commit false speech for the sake of protecting another.
One does not commit harsh speech for the sake of subduing others;
one does not commit divisive speech for the sake of destroying the heterodox views, false inflation, or arrogance of outsiders;
and one does not commit frivolous speech because there is no one to whom it is appropriate to address it.
To commit anger without harsh or abusive instruction;
to lack the aspiration for superior roots of goodness, which is termed greed;
and to harbor improper thoughts toward those who are self-reliant and protective, committing wrong views with even a few unrighteous words.
Kāśyapa! If one does not stubbornly cling to these ten paths of unwholesome action, I do not say that they are called "faults. Kāśyapa!
If one does not remain firmly attached to these ten paths of unwholesome action, it is called non-offense.
In this same way, Kāśyapa,
if all afflictions are not firmly attached, I say there is no offense.
“Kāśyapa!
Those who do not cling are called ‘those who have left behind views. Kāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!
Among the ten paths of unwholesome karma, which is the most grave?
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! Among these ten paths of unwholesome action, killing and wrong view are called the most grave.
Kāśyapa!”

Wherever there may be various evils and unwholesome states, if one does not dwell firmly in them, does not cling to them firmly, or does not adhere to them firmly, I declare that all such cases constitute non-transgression.

Kāśyapa! Whether it be a minor unwholesome act, if one dwells firmly upon it, clings to it tenaciously, or adheres to it with persistence, I declare that all such instances constitute an offense. Kāśyapa!

If one does not remain firm, cling firmly, or adhere firmly to the five deeds of immediate retribution, but gives rise to [right] views, I do not say that such a person is called an offender, much less for other minor unwholesome paths of action.
Kāśyapa! I do not attain bodhi by means of unwholesome dharmas;
nor do I attain bodhi by means of wholesome dharmas.
Kāśyapa! If one were to attain bodhi through unwholesome states, then all ordinary worldlings would also attain bodhi;
if one were to attain bodhi through wholesome dharmas, then all grasses, trees, shrubs, and forests that have been burned should grow back once more.
“Kāśyapa!
I now ask you: how does a Tathāgata attain bodhi?
Kāśyapa replied:
“The Buddha is the root of the Dharma; the World-Honored One is the eye; the World-Honored One is the refuge. As the World-Honored One has taught, we shall together practice accordingly.
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!
To understand that afflictions arise from causes and conditions is called attaining bodhi.
Kāśyapa, what is meant by understanding that afflictions arise from causes and conditions?
To understand that these phenomena arise without intrinsic nature and are unarisen—understanding them in this way is called attaining bodhi.
Kāśyapa, it is merely by way of provisional names that one is said to attain bodhi; yet this bodhi is not attained through letters or verbal expression.
If there are no words, no speech, and no discourse, and no attainment of bodhi,
this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Kāśyapa, as to what you have asked:
"Which of the ten paths of unwholesome action is the most grave? "Kāśyapa!
Suppose a man has a father who has attained the path of a pratyekabuddha; if the son takes his father's life, this is called the gravest among acts of killing."
To seize the property of the Triple Gem is the gravest among forms of theft;
if there is another person who commits impurity with his mother—who has left the household life and attained the path of Arhatship—that is the gravest among forms of sexual misconduct;
and to slander the Tathāgata with falsehoods is the gravest among forms of lying.
If one uses divisive speech to cause schism within the assembly of noble sages, this is the gravest form of divisive speech;
if one reviles a holy person, this is the gravest form of harsh speech;
and if one speaks to confuse and disrupt those who seek the Dharma, this is the gravest form of frivolous speech.
If one commits the initial act of the five heinous crimes, this is the most severe form of hatred;
if one seeks to plunder those who uphold the pure precepts, this is the most severe form of greed and the most severe form of wrong view—namely, what is called the "extreme view."
Kāśyapa! These ten paths of unwholesome action are the most grave. Kāśyapa!
The Tathāgata knows that these ten unwholesome karmas are the most grave.
Kāśyapa! If there is a person who possesses these ten unwholesome acts, Kāśyapa!

If these evil sentient beings understand that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of causes and conditions—that within this there is no sentient being, no life-span, no person, no man, no self, no youth, no doer, and no receiver or arouser;
that there is no knower or seer, no *pudgala*;
that there is no arising, no ceasing, and no conditioned activity—this is the dharma of exhaustion, which is unstained, unattached, devoid of good or evil, and pure by its very nature.

"Kāśyapa! All dharmas are by nature eternally pure; if one understands, knows, and enters into this with faith, I do not say that such a person will go toward the evil realms, nor shall they experience the fruits of the evil realms."
Why is this? Kāśyapa!
The Dharma has no accumulation; the Dharma has no gathering and no affliction.
Kāśyapa! All dharmas arise and perish without abiding; they come into being through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and having arisen, they return to extinction. Kāśyapa!
If the mind arises and ceases, all fetters and afflictions likewise arise and then cease;
if one understands it in this way, there is no transgression nor any locus for transgression. Kāśyapa!
If one were to commit an offense and yet remain [in a state of purity], such a thing is impossible. Kāśyapa!

It is as if there were a great dark room for a hundred thousand years where no lamp has been lit; this extremely dark room has no doors, windows, or openings, nor even a hole as small as a needle’s eye through which the light of the sun, moon, jewels, or fire could enter. No light whatsoever can penetrate it.
Kāśyapa!
If a lamp is lit in a dark room, could that darkness possibly say:
"I have dwelt here for hundreds of thousands of years; you should not depart now"?
Kāśyapa replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
"Of course, when it is lamp-light, darkness has already departed.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Kāśyapa!"

Regarding the karmic obstructions created over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, if one has faith in the Tathāgata’s words, understands the dharma of conditions, cultivates the practice of observation, and cultivates meditative concentration and wisdom—observing that there is no self, no life-principle, no person, no individual, and so forth—I declare that such a person is called "without transgression," "without locus," and "without accumulation."
Kāśyapa! For this reason, you should know that when the lamp of wisdom shines, weak and inferior afflictions are unable to remain. "Kāśyapa!"

This is called the unsurpassed dwelling place of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; it is the Great Lion’s Roar that turns the pure wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by devas, humans, māras, or brahmās.
Kāśyapa!
If there are sentient beings who have faith in this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, and who uphold it and contemplate it in this way, they shall let out such a great lion’s roar.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since this Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve has offered his own body as an offering to the Tathāgata, by what kind of body will he awaken to the path of bodhi?”
At that time, the bodhisattvas within the lotus pedestal asked Ānanda:
"What do you think?
Can awakening (bodhi) be realized through the body?"
"Ānanda! Do not hold such a view (you should awaken to bodhi through both body and mind).
Ānanda replied:
"O noble sons! If bodhi is not awakened to by means of body and mind, by what else should one awaken to bodhi?
The Bodhisattvas replied:
"Venerable Ānanda!

The true nature of the body is the true nature of bodhi; the true nature of bodhi is the true nature of the mind; and the true nature of the mind is the true nature of all dharmas. To awaken to all these true natures is therefore called awakening to bodhi."
Then all the bodhisattvas on the lotus pedestals prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
When we arrive at this great earth, it will be that the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When will these bodhisattvas and the multitude of flower-pedestals arrive at this great earth?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These bodhisattvas, in the regions below, have consulted with and questioned as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges regarding this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury; having heard it, they have understood its meaning."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
After how much time will this Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha told Ānanda: “Ānanda!
Among these thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa who have already appeared or are yet to appear, the last Tathāgata shall be named Lu-zhi (Ruci).”
Ānanda! The assembly of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Lu-zhi is, for the most part, greater than the śrāvaka saṃghas of all previous Buddhas. Ānanda!
Then the Tathāgata Lu-zhi (Ruci) bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Wuliangzhi Zhuangyanwang (Anantamati-vyūharāja) the prediction of unsurpassed awakening, saying:

"After ninety-eight kalpas have passed, the Bodhisattva Anantamati-vyūharāja shall attain Buddhahood; he shall be named Zhuangyanwang (Vyūharāja), and he too shall realize the unsurpassed way within this very realm."

"When the Tathāgata King Adorned sits upon this ground, all the bodhisattvas within these flower pedestals shall likewise reach the ground and further hear this Dharma of the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata."
Ānanda! At that time, the world-system of the Tathāgata King Adorned was named Immeasurable Merit Adornment. Ānanda!
All the celestial palaces of the desire realm are equal to but a single jewel terrace within the Buddha-land of King Adorned;
at that time, this Sahā world shall be named the Land of Exquisite Colors.

Ānanda! The Tathāgata King Adorned will have a lifespan of one hundred kalpas; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma will remain in the world for a full ten kalpas, consisting entirely of a saṃgha of bodhisattvas.

When the Tathāgata Adorned King had finished bestowing this prophecy, the flower-canopy of that buddha-field vanished and was no longer seen; instead, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Resolve Adorned King appeared before the Buddha and stood there.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

How may this Dharma be protected and upheld so that it may endure for a long time, spreading and flourishing throughout Jambudvīpa? How may those virtuous men who are able to uphold the Tathāgata’s secret treasury of Dharma fulfill their merits and obtain this teaching?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Even if the four great elements were to change their natures, I would never allow these good men to pass away without having heard this Dharma."
Ānanda! If there are those who copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, you should know that such persons are sustained by the Tathāgata. Ānanda!

If there were someone who, with their right hand, held seven treasures filling Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and with their left hand likewise held seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and if they practiced such giving three times during the day and three times at night, continuing without weariness for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—Ānanda!
This is the merit of such giving;
however, for those who copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain shall exceed even this!
Therefore, Ānanda!

You should now receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, so that all who are vessels of the Dharma may hear and know it; these people will then be upholding the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva King Adorned with Immeasurable Resolve, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Kāśyapa, and the entire great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Vaipulya Sūtra on the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata, Scroll II.
